title: env-cap: capability-owned environment contracts
description: Every environment variable has an owner, a reason to exist, and a lifecycle you can query. env-cap treats configuration as a capability-owned contract, not loose strings read off process.env. It sits next to your existing validation, not instead of it.
maturity: env-cap is pre-1.0. Before 1.0, a minor release may break the Stable tier ([VERSIONING.md](https://github.com/maverickcer/env-cap/blob/main/VERSIONING.md)). Pin a version and read the changelog on every minor.

hero.heading: Every environment variable has an owner, a reason to exist, and a lifecycle you can query.
hero.lede: A secret manager decides where a value lives. A validator decides whether it is well-formed. Neither says who owns it, why it exists, or when it expires.
hero.support: Each part of your code declares the variables it owns. A build step turns those declarations into an ownership and lifecycle report.
hero.outcome: Give every team a clear owner and expiry date for each environment variable, alongside the validator and secret manager you already use.

install.label: Quick start
install.note: The runtime validates your variables at startup. The build step produces the ownership report. Nothing replaces `dotenv`, Zod, `envalid`, `t3-env` or your secret manager.

problem.heading: Secret managers and validators answer different questions.
problem.lede: A secret manager decides where a value lives. A validator decides whether it is well-formed. Neither says why a variable exists, who owns it, or whether it is still needed.
items: a leftover from a feature that moved on
problem.closing: env-cap puts the answer in the code. Each capability declares the variables it owns, and a build step turns the declarations into one project-wide view.

model.heading: Runtime and build-time stay separate on purpose.
model.lede: The runtime has no filesystem access and imports no Node module. Build tooling creates the visibility needed to maintain dependencies, as an explicit development or CI step, never at startup.
flow: → Build path: `documentEnv()` · static AST analysis, never imported or executed · generated manifest, docs and ownership report
model.flowDescription: A capability's schema file branches into a runtime path for validated application access and a build path for generated documentation and visibility artifacts.
model.note: The build package parses schema files as TypeScript ASTs and never imports or executes them. That static-analysis boundary stops unfamiliar code from running as a side effect of generating documentation, manifests and dependency insight.

demo.heading: Output from examples/application.
demo.intro: In [examples/application](https://github.com/maverickcer/env-cap/tree/main/examples/application), `npx env-cap --include src/env.ts --location src/generated/env.manifest.ts --evidence docs/env.evidence.json` prints the first lines. `npx tsx scripts/generate-docs/run.ts` prints the rest.
demo.output:
$ npx env-cap --include src/env.ts --location src/generated/env.manifest.ts --evidence docs/env.evidence.json
Wrote manifest: src/generated/env.manifest.ts
Discovered 1 contract(s).
Wrote evidence: docs/env.evidence.json

$ npx tsx scripts/generate-docs/run.ts
[generate-docs] wrote docs/ENVIRONMENT.md (1 contract(s)), .env.example, and docs/OWNERSHIP.md (0 abandoned, 2 unconsumed owned variable(s)).

1 variable(s)/contract(s) expiring soon or already expired:
  - STRIPE_KEY in env: 2026-09-01 (expired Nd ago)

2 unconsumed owned variable(s):
  - DATABASE_URL in app
  - STRIPE_KEY in app
demo.explanation: An expiry date that has passed, and two variables a contract declares but nothing reads. The first comes from a declaration; the second is computed from the syntax tree. N is the number of days since 2026-09-01, counted on the day you run it.

guarantees.heading: What is enforced, and where it stops.
guarantees.lede: Each claim names what enforces it and where it stops, and links to the document that defines it.

items.claim: The runtime has no filesystem access and imports no Node module.
items.scope: Lint and a tarball scan enforce the first; a browser-bundle test the second. The build entry loads a bundled TypeScript 6 compiler, and a build step fails if a runtime entry can reach it.

items.claim: The build tool never executes your schema files.
items.scope: Schema files are parsed as TypeScript syntax trees, never imported or evaluated, and a test proves a throwing statement never runs. Only literal values are resolved; anything dynamic is reported as unresolved. It does not sandbox the rest of your build.

items.claim: The runtime never stores, fetches or rotates secrets, and keeps values out of its errors.
items.scope: No code for storing or fetching secrets exists; that is a statement about the source, not a check. A message your own validator builds from the value is passed through. Spreading a contract reads every value.

comparison.eyebrow: Why not dotenv, Zod, envalid or t3-env?
comparison.heading: You keep all of them.
comparison.lede: env-cap does not replace your loader or your validator. It adds the layer none of them cover. Plug an existing `Validator<T>` or `Processor<T>` function into a contract, or use env-cap's helpers when a validation library is more than a variable needs.
comparison.caption: Where common approaches stop and env-cap begins
rows: Loads values from a `.env` file into `process.env`
Says nothing about who owns a value, whether it's still used, or when it expires
Validates that a value has the right shape
Same gap: a well-typed variable can still be an orphaned, unowned, or expired one
Decides where a value physically lives and how it's rotated
Says nothing about which capability in your code actually depends on it

adoption.heading: From one schema to capability-owned contracts.
adoption.lede: Most applications start with a single, centralized schema, and that is a fine place to stay if it's working. As ownership boundaries start to matter, contracts move closer to the capability that consumes them, with no change to the runtime model.
adoption.calloutTitle: A progressive path, not a rewrite
steps: Start with one centralized schema and run `npx env-cap init`.
Generate the manifest, documentation and ownership report in CI.
As ownership boundaries matter, move each contract next to the capability that consumes it. The runtime model does not change.

notFor.title: You probably don't need it when
notFor.text: Your application is small, one team owns every configuration decision, environment variables are few and stable, and you already have enough visibility into your dependencies. A validation library alone, or plain `dotenv`, may be all you need.

brief.heading: A one-page brief for your manager
brief.oneLine: env-cap gives every configuration setting an owner, a reason to exist and an expiry date, and shows what is unused or overdue.
brief.problem: As an application grows, nobody can say who owns a setting, whether it is still used, or when a secret expires. That knowledge sits in wikis, chat threads and people's memory.
brief.whatItDoes: Each part of the application declares the settings it owns. A build step reports owners, unused settings and coming expiry dates. The application checks its settings when it starts.
whyItMatters: Overdue secret rotations and orphaned settings are found by a report, not by an outage.
It works alongside the validator and secret manager a team already has, so nothing is replaced.
The part that runs in your application imports no Node module and stays under 3 KB compressed.
brief.whatItCosts: Adopting it in one application means adding the package and declaring the settings each part of the code owns. It is free, open source software under the MIT licence, and it replaces no existing tool.
whatCouldGoWrong: Its reports are only as accurate as the declarations a team writes, and it cannot see settings read from outside the code it scans.
Security fixes target the latest 0.x release only, and there is no backport branch before 1.0.
The install includes a TypeScript 6 compiler, used only to build the reports.
brief.whatWeAsk: Agree that one application trials it for a few weeks, then judge from its ownership report whether to spread it.
